t.1.66.1: Addressed thus by her, Śakra gave instructions to Sadāgati, the ever-moving Wind; then, at the proper time, Menakā set out together with Vāyu.
t.1.66.2: Then the fair-hipped, timid Menakā saw Viśvāmitra in his hermitage, practicing austerities, his sins burnt away by his asceticism.
t.1.66.3: Then, having saluted him, she began to play in the presence of the seer, and the wind carried away her garment, which shone like the moon.
t.1.66.5: Then the best of sages saw Menakā laid bare, flustered and clutching eagerly at her garment, a woman whose youth and beauty were beyond description.
t.1.66.6: Then, having seen the excellence of her beauty, that bull among Brahmins, fallen under the sway of desire, set his heart on union with her.
t.1.66.4: The lovely-complexioned woman hurried to the ground, clutching at that garment, and seemed to smile bashfully at Māruta.
t.1.66.7: He invited her, and she, the blameless one, desired him too. The two of them dallied there in the forest for a very long time, delighting in each other as they pleased, and it seemed to them but a single day.
t.1.66.8: That sage begot Śakuntalā upon Menakā on a lovely tableland of Himavat, near the river Mālinī.
t.1.66.10: Seeing that infant lying in the desolate forest teeming with lions and tigers, birds surrounded it on all sides.
t.1.66.9: Having abandoned that newborn child on the bank of the Mālinī, Menakā, her task accomplished, then swiftly went to the assembly of Śakra.
t.1.66.11: So that flesh-eating beasts greedy for meat might not harm this little girl in the forest, the birds guarded her there, the daughter of Menakā.
t.1.66.12: Having gone to perform my ablutions, I saw her lying in a lonely, desolate forest, surrounded by śakunta birds. Then, having brought her here, I appointed her to the status of my daughter.
t.1.66.14: And because in the desolate forest she was guarded by birds, the name Śakuntalā was therefore given to her by me.
t.1.66.13: He who begets the body, he who saves one's life, and he whose food one eats: these three, in that order, are all declared to be fathers in the settled judgment of dharma.
t.1.66.15: Thus, gentle one, know Śakuntalā to be my daughter; and the blameless Śakuntalā regards me as her father.
t.1.66.17: For I regard Kaṇva as my father, not knowing my own father. Thus, O king, I have told you what happened, just as I heard it.
t.1.66.16: When he was asked, he told this account of my birth to a great seer. Know me, then, O lord of men, to be the daughter of Kaṇva.
